title: Canada's budget funds a new online safety regulator that would cover AI chatbots
excerpt: Canada's Budget 2026, released on 5 November, sets aside money for a commission to enforce new duties on social media and AI chatbots, and floats a body to test advanced AI.

sources.title: Government of Canada: Budget 2026, Chapter 5: A safe and sovereign Canada

iPhone in Canada: Budget 2026: What changes for cell phones, AI and tech in Canada (5 November 2026)

body_html:
Canada's federal government released its Budget 2026 on 5 November 2026. Alongside large spending on computing capacity, it includes money for a new regulator that would oversee safety duties for social media services and AI chatbot services, and a commitment to explore an international body that would check whether advanced AI models stay under human control.

None of this is law yet. The duties come from bills that are still before Parliament, and the budget's own wording on the international body is a promise to explore, not a decision.

A regulator for chatbots and social media

The budget proposes C$176.3 million over five years, starting in the 2026-27 financial year, and C$29.3 million a year after that, for the Department of Canadian Heritage to set up a Digital Safety and Data Protection Commission of Canada. The commission would enforce Bill C-34, the Safe Social Media Act, which the government introduced in June 2026.

According to the budget, Bill C-34 sets "new requirements for social media services and AI chatbot services." Its main elements include:

  • A duty to protect children: services would have to build in design features aimed at protecting children from harm.
  • A duty to act responsibly: services would assess risks across seven categories of harmful content and label content that has been generated synthetically.
  • Specific chatbot duties: the budget says AI chatbot services would have specific requirements "aimed at reducing the risks of harmful content and behaviour."
  • Reporting tools: users would get accessible ways to report harmful material.

A possible body to test advanced AI

The budget says Canada will work with other countries to explore creating a new body, such as a "Technology Stability Board", that would assess whether advanced AI models are safe and remain under human control. No structure, budget or timetable for it is given.

Separately, the budget proposes C$6.2 million over four years, starting in 2027-28, so that Canada can stay involved in GPAI, an international forum on AI where governments share information and build practical tools.

What is not in the budget

Canada still has no general AI law. Its earlier proposal, the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act, lapsed without becoming law, and the budget does not propose a replacement. Bill C-36, a privacy bill also introduced in June 2026, would add stronger protections for children and more transparency about personal information used in automated systems.

It is not yet known when Parliament will vote on Bills C-34 and C-36, how the chatbot duties would be written in detail, or when the commission would start work.

Why it matters for staying in charge

Chatbots are increasingly treated by lawmakers as products with safety duties, not only as websites. Canada's approach puts weight on design choices for children, on labelling machine-made content so people know what they are looking at (D4 Honest identity), and on having a named regulator that can hold services to account (D9 Accountable).

The proposed testing body goes to the most basic question of all: can people still stop and steer the most capable systems (D1 Always stoppable)? Whether it happens will depend on agreement with other countries.
